meta.description: Quote Investigator: the first instances are anonymous. The kernel was in print by 1905, the full wording by 1930. The Ambrose Bierce credit dates from 1999.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A Banker Lends You His Umbrella When It's Sunny and Wants It Back When It Rains'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Bierce. QI traces the joke to anonymous print, 1905-1930; Bierce's name was attached in a 1999 Bernanke paper. It is not in The Devil's Dictionary.

answer.label: Not Ambrose Bierce — an anonymous banking joke
answer.authorDates: Kernel in print by April 1905 · full wording by January 1930 · originator never identified
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that “the first instances of this maxim are anonymous” and that Mark Twain, Robert Frost and Ambrose Bierce were all “implausibly attached to the quotation” years later. The kernel of the idea turns up in a London accountancy weekly in April 1905, and the full-fledged wording in The Journal of Business of the University of Chicago in January 1930 — credited there to nobody but “some person of shrewd wit.” The line appears nowhere in The Devil’s Dictionary, and the earliest credit to Bierce that QI located is a 1999 economics paper.

source.heading: Where the joke actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Ambrose Bierce — and, just as often, Mark Twain, Robert Frost, Ralph Waldo Emerson or Philip La Follette
The Accountant: The Recognised Weekly Organ of Chartered Accountants

London, 15 April 1905, page 464 — “Notes on a Banker’s Accounts” by John Moodie, a paper read to the Manchester Chartered Accountants Society on 10 March 1905. The remark is quoted from an unnamed customer, not coined by the author.

docMeta.dt: Earliest full wording found by QI
docMeta.dd: The Journal of Business of the University of Chicago, vol. III no. 1, January 1930, page 21, in Lionel D. Edie’s “The Banks and the Stock Market Crisis of 1929” — where it is credited only to “some person of shrewd wit”

source.excerpt: Some person of shrewd wit has given a definition of a banker which, though a bit severe, nevertheless strikes a responsive chord. A banker, according to this definition, is a fellow who lends you his umbrella when the sun is shining and insists upon its return as soon as it starts to rain.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ is the anchor. Its verdict: “the first instances of this maxim are anonymous. Years later, famous people such as Mark Twain, Robert Frost, and Ambrose Bierce were implausibly attached to the quotation. The core idea appeared by 1905, and the full fledged quotation entered circulation by 1930.”

The 1905 kernel, as QI transcribes it from The Accountant of 15 April 1905, is a bank customer’s grumble reported by an accountant: “A customer who was not getting what he wanted, once said to me: ‘You bankers only lend a man an umbrella when it is a fine day,’ and I thought he expressed it exactly.” Barry Popik’s parallel file ↗ picks the trail up in 1930 and adds two 1932 sightings, listing Emerson, Twain, Frost and Philip La Follette as claimants — and never once mentioning Bierce.

The Bierce credit can be dated precisely. On page 8 of NBER Working Paper 7559 ↗, Ben Bernanke and Mark Gertler write that credit flows more freely to borrowers already in strong shape, “hence Ambrose Bierce’s definition of a banker as someone who lends you an umbrella when the sun is shining and wants it back when it starts to rain.” The paper was given at Jackson Hole in August 1999 and issued by the NBER in February 2000; it offers no source for the Bierce credit.

The negative check is decisive. Searching the complete text of The Devil’s Dictionary ↗ returns no “umbrella” and no “parasol”, and there is no headword for bank, banker or banking. “Banker” occurs once in the entire book, inside the entry for RAREBIT. Wikiquote’s Bierce page ↗, which does keep a Misattributed section, does not list the line at all.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest full-fledged version of the saying that Quote Investigator located, transcribed by QI from the January 1930 issue and marked “Verified on microfilm”. Note what the writer — Lionel D. Edie, analysing the 1929 crash — does with it: he introduces it as something “some person of shrewd wit has given,” the phrasing of a man repeating a line already in circulation. He names nobody. Neither Bierce nor Twain nor Frost is anywhere near it.

source.rightsNote: No copyright status can be asserted for the sentence that circulates, because no author and no first publication have ever been identified for it — Quote Investigator’s earliest instances are all anonymous. The two printings closest to the origin (The Accountant, April 1905, and The Journal of Business of the University of Chicago, January 1930) both predate 1931 and would be long out of copyright in the United States, but neither names an author and neither is the sentence quote sites hang on Bierce.

author.name: Ambrose Bierce
author.kicker: About the name it travels under
author.heading: Ambrose Bierce
author.metaLine: 1842–c. 1914 · American journalist, Civil War veteran & satirist
author.bio: Ambrose Bierce (born 24 June 1842) was a Union Army veteran turned San Francisco newspaperman, short-story writer and satirist, best known for An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge and for the mordant lexicon first published in October 1906 as The Cynic’s Word Book and reissued in 1911 as The Devil’s Dictionary. He was last heard from in a letter dated 26 December 1913, written from Chihuahua, Mexico, and is generally given as having died around 1914. That reputation — the man who wrote cynical dictionary definitions — is precisely why an ownerless cynical dictionary definition eventually landed on him; but the words “umbrella” and “parasol” do not occur anywhere in The Devil’s Dictionary, which has no entry for bank or banker at all.

misattribution.heading: How an ownerless joke collected four famous fathers
misattribution.intro: This is a saying with no author and an unusually crowded list of claimants. Quote Investigator ↗ tracks the credits arriving decades after the joke was already common property, each one attaching a famous name to a line that had been circulating unsigned.

items.why: The earliest Bierce credit QI ↗ located is from 1999, in a paper by Ben Bernanke and Mark Gertler; the same sentence appears on page 8 of NBER Working Paper 7559 ↗. Bierce was last heard from in a letter dated 26 December 1913. And the line is absent from his work: the full text of The Devil’s Dictionary ↗ has no “umbrella”, no “parasol” and no bank or banker headword. Wikiquote’s Bierce page ↗ does not carry it either, in any section.

The first Twain credit QI ↗ found is Bennett Cerf’s anecdote collection Try and Stop Me, page 241, in 1944 — a full fourteen years after the definition was already in print unsigned. TwainQuotes ↗ lists the line with a standing notice that “until the attribution can be verified, the quote should not be regarded as authentic.”

In 1949 the collector Evan Esar put the saying in The Dictionary of Humorous Quotations twice over — once under Twain and once, in a different wording (“A bank is a place where they lend you an umbrella in fair weather and ask for it back again when it begins to rain”), under Frost. QI ↗ records both entries. A joke credited to two different men in the same book is a joke belonging to neither.

The earliest full printing, from January 1930, reads “lends you his umbrella when the sun is shining and insists upon its return as soon as it starts to rain.” The smoother sentence that circulates today — “wants it back the minute it begins to rain” — is the form Esar printed under Twain’s name in 1949 ↗, and the one TwainQuotes ↗ carries. The still shorter “wants it back when it rains” is a modern compression, and it is also the form Quote Investigator uses as its own page title.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who made the joke. Quote Investigator ↗’s conclusion is that “the first instances of this maxim are anonymous” and that Twain, Frost and Bierce were “implausibly attached to the quotation” only afterwards — the core idea by 1905, the full quotation in circulation by 1930, and the famous names from 1944 onward.

context.heading: A joke that grew, then went looking for a father
lead: The saying did not arrive fully formed. Its earliest documented ancestor, in a paper on bankers’ accounts read to the Manchester Chartered Accountants Society in March 1905 and printed in The Accountant that April, is not an aphorism at all — it is a complaint. The author reports that a customer who had been refused what he wanted said to him, “You bankers only lend a man an umbrella when it is a fine day,” and adds, “I thought he expressed it exactly.” The wit belongs to an unnamed bank customer in Edwardian Manchester.

Twenty-five years later the joke had been polished into a definition. In January 1930, weeks after the Wall Street crash, an article in The Journal of Business of the University of Chicago introduced it as something “some person of shrewd wit has given” — a writer passing along a line already in circulation and unable to say whose it was. That is the shape of a proverb, not of an authored epigram. Famous names only started arriving in the 1940s, once the joke was common property and needed a signature.
detailsBody: The Bierce test is easy to run and it fails cleanly. The complete text of The Devil’s Dictionary on Project Gutenberg ↗ — the 1911 A-to-Z version, running to around a thousand definitions — contains the word “umbrella” zero times and “parasol” zero times, and has no headword for bank, banker or banking. The word “banker” occurs exactly once in the whole book, buried in the entry for RAREBIT, in a gag about riz-de-veau à la financière not being “the smile of a calf prepared after the recipe of a she banker.”

One intriguing near-relative is French. In October 1928, reviewing Philippe Girardet’s Les Affaires et les Hommes for the journal Books Abroad, Harold A. Larrabee of Union College translated Girardet’s definition of a banker as “a man who will gladly lend you a parasol when the sun shines, but who pitilessly refuses you an umbrella when it rains.” The two-object version is sharper than the one that survived, and it is the closest thing to a named author anywhere in the chain — but it predates the English aphorism by only two years and postdates the 1905 kernel by twenty-three, so it reads as another branch of the same joke rather than its root. Quote Investigator ↗ records it without claiming it as the origin, and neither do we.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI concludes the first instances are anonymous and that Twain, Frost and Bierce were implausibly attached; documents The Accountant 15 Apr 1905 p.464 (John Moodie), Books Abroad Oct 1928 (Girardet/Larrabee parasol version), The Journal of Business of the University of Chicago Jan 1930 p.21 (Lionel D. Edie, 'some person of shrewd wit'), The International Digest Dec 1930, Bennett Cerf's Try and Stop Me 1944 p.241 as first Twain credit, Evan Esar 1949 crediting both Twain and Frost, and Bernanke & Gertler 1999 crediting Ambrose Bierce.

Page 8 reads: 'hence Ambrose Bierce's definition of a banker as someone who lends you an umbrella when the sun is shining and wants it back when it starts to rain'. Paper is NBER Working Paper 7559, February 2000, presented at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City Jackson Hole conference, August 26-28, 1999.

The complete text of The Devil's Dictionary contains zero occurrences of 'umbrella' and zero of 'parasol', has no headword for bank/banker/banking, and contains the word 'banker' exactly once, inside the entry for RAREBIT ('the smile of a calf prepared after the recipe of a she banker').

TwainQuotes lists 'A banker is a fellow who lends you his umbrella when the sun is shining and wants it back the minute it begins to rain' with the note: 'This quote has been attributed to Mark Twain, but until the attribution can be verified, the quote should not be regarded as authentic.'

Barry Popik's entry documents the December 1930 International Digest wording plus 1932 citations (Bulletin of the Robert Morris Associates vol. 15-16 p.84; Lodi CA Sentinel, 25 Feb 1932, p.2) and lists Ralph Waldo Emerson, Mark Twain, Robert Frost and Philip La Follette as claimants; Ambrose Bierce is not mentioned anywhere in the entry.

Wikiquote's Ambrose Bierce page has sections for What I Saw At Shiloh (1881), The Cynic's Word Book (1906), The Devil's Dictionary (1911), Epigrams and Misattributed, and does not contain the banker/umbrella quotation in any section.

Ambrose Bierce was born 24 June 1842 in Meigs County, Ohio; his last known communication is a letter dated 26 December 1913 written from Chihuahua, Mexico, to Blanche Partington; his death is given as c. 1914. He was a Union Army veteran, journalist and satirist.

The work was first published in book form in October 1906 as The Cynic's Word Book (Doubleday, Page & Co., 521 definitions, A-L) and published under the title The Devil's Dictionary in 1911 as Volume 7 of The Collected Works of Ambrose Bierce (Neale Publishing Company, 1,013 definitions, full alphabet).
